title: Unleashing Emergent Fermions with Rydberg Atom Simulators
authors: Hanteng Wang, Xingyu Li, Shang Liu, Yingfei Gu, Chengshu Li
abstract: Rydberg atom simulators, in both analog and digital modes, have attracted significant recent interest due to their versatile geometric reconfigurability. In this work, leveraging this feature, we propose two complementary approaches, one for each mode, to characterize emergent fermions in critical quantum many-body systems. In the analog mode, we assemble the Rydberg atoms in a "developable" (namely, preserving local couplings) Möbius band geometry to realize antiperiodic boundary conditions, where fermionic states reside. Spectroscopic measurement in this sector then reveals universal energy ratios of the bosonic and fermionic states. In the digital mode, we carry out a fermionic version of Kibble-Zurek ramping with a quantum circuit, directly addressing the fermionic scaling form. Reconfigurability allows an exponential speed-up of this task, with an $O(\log L\log\log L)$ circuit-depth overhead. Our work establishes the Rydberg atom simulator as a uniquely powerful platform to attack the notoriously difficult issue of experimentally probing emergent fermions that are nonlocally defined in a bosonic system.
summary: The paper details two advanced protocols—one analog and one digital—to use Rydberg atom simulators to experimentally investigate emergent fermionic excitations in bosonic quantum systems. By leveraging geometric reconfigurability, they achieve state-of-the-art circuit depth scaling for simulating non-local dynamics. This establishes the platform as a powerful tool for testing fundamental concepts from condensed matter theory.
main_problem: To experimentally probe emergent fermions that are nonlocally defined within a bosonic quantum many-body system, particularly by characterizing critical phenomena and scaling dimensions.
main_result: The authors propose complementary analog (Möbius band) and digital (Kibble-Zurek ramping) protocols using Rydberg atom simulators to verify conformal invariance and establish the platform's capability for probing emergent fermionic excitations.
method: The work combines theoretical analysis of boundary conditions (APBC vs. OBC) with quantum simulation techniques, including implementing complex non-local gates via binary-tree compression on programmable qubit arrays.
model_or_system: The primary platform is the Rydberg atom simulator, which can realize both analog and digital protocols. The physics involves studying critical points (TCI class) where emergent fermionic degrees of freedom are expected to appear in an otherwise bosonic system.
key_observables: Universal energy ratios ($\epsilon, \epsilon', \psi$), fermionic Kibble-Zurek scaling exponent ($\chi$), and the dynamical Binder ratio collapse.
important_parameters: The geometry (Möbius band vs. cylinder), the perturbation strength ($h$), system size ($L$), and critical exponents ($\psi$).
main_assumptions: In the analog mode, realizing a developable Möbius band geometry is assumed. In the digital mode, Open Boundary Conditions are crucial for isolating the fermionic scaling dimension $[\psi]$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of both protocols (Möbius band/Qubit array), finite-size scaling collapses confirming predicted exponents ($\chi$), and detailed circuit diagrams showing $O(\log L \log \log L)$ gate depth via binary-tree compression.
paper_structure: The paper is structured around two complementary approaches: the analog method using geometric constraints (Möbius band) to enforce antiperiodic boundary conditions, and the digital method employing quantum circuits for dynamic probing (Kibble-Zurek). A significant portion details the advanced quantum circuit compilation techniques required for non-local gates.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of experimental realization in AMO physics by mapping abstract theoretical concepts (emergent fermions, CFT) onto a programmable hardware platform (Rydberg atoms), while simultaneously advancing the computational methods needed to simulate these complex interactions.
